I left Windows for good years ago. I use Ubuntu, I don't hate Unity like everyone else and I disabled the Amazon shit so it's fine. It's the most "out of the box" and most consistent in getting all peripherals to work. Just install a dual boot and keep Windows for "just in case" scenarios. After a while you'll find you don't need it at all.

For most Windows users interesting in moving over to Linux-based operating systems, I will typically recommend the KDE desktop environment, as it is similar to the standard Windows shell in appearance, as well as being highly customizable, with hundreds of themes to chose from if you don't feel like making your own.

As far as the gaming situation goes, it's not too bad, and it is improving with time. I currently have two versions of steam installed. One of them is the native Linux client, and the other is the Windows client running in Wine. So far, most of the games that I run within wine are perfectly playable, with the odd glitch here and there.

Most of the other applications that you requested might be tried in wine, but if they don't work, I might suggest looking into these Linux alternatives: (They might not have all of the exact same functions or features, but they might be worth a try)

  • Photoshop - GNU Image Manipulation Program

  • FL Studio - Linux MultiMedia Studio

  • Paint Tool SAI - MyPaint

And as far as your keypad goes, I'm not too sure. In my personal experience, most of the peripherals that I have tried where plug-and-play, and just worked. I haven't had to hunt for drivers once so far. This includes all of the mice, gamepads and webcams that I have used.

I made the switch from Windows / MacOSX to Ubuntu full time about 3-4 years ago, and I haven't looked back. The experience has been relatively smooth sailing for me so far, and it gives one a feeling of newfound freedom, being able to tinker with things, experiment and customize your machine in any which way you like. I recommended diving in and giving it a shot. Best of luck.

First try Mint as a Live instance (USB or DVD). This will allow you to test whether it works for your hardware before you commit anything to disk. Next, install Mint alongside Windows as a dual boot machine. The Mint installer can do this for you for most hardware. When you boot up, you will be given a choice betseen Windows and Linux.
I would try it in a VM first, try a few flavores then decide if you want to cross over. Also give up your gmail, spotify, google searches, and Amazon account if your worried about privacy.

My advise for those that want to try Linux:

USB3 performance is in the same league as HD performance.

  1. Buy a USB3 flashdrive of at least 4 GB. (~15 dollar)

  3. Select a distribution from the list at 'step 1' and select 'download' if you don't already have it.
  4. Select the distribution-location at 'step 2' and the flash drive at 'step 3'
  5. At 'step 4' you can choose if you want to be able to make changes to your system once it is installed, and how much space to reserve for that.
  6. _Finished. Have fun with your new Linux computer :D
